title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is a 1948 proclamation, not a treaty
body:
## What the United Nations says the document is

The United Nations page on the Universal Declaration states that the General Assembly proclaimed it in Paris on 10 December 1948, as General Assembly resolution 217 A, "as a common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations." The page says it was drafted by representatives with different legal and cultural backgrounds from all regions, that it has been translated into over 500 languages, and that it inspired and paved the way for more than seventy human rights treaties that refer to it in their preambles.

A proclamation of a common standard is not, by that description, itself a treaty. Treaties that came later are what states ratify. This card does not list those treaties, because their texts were not the page that was read.

## Two articles, quoted because the wording is the law-like content

Article 1: "All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. They are endowed with reason and conscience and should act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood."

Article 11, paragraph 1: "Everyone charged with a penal offence has the right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law in a public trial at which he has had all the guarantees necessary for his defence."

The preamble ties the declaration to "barbarous acts which have outraged the conscience of mankind." That is the Assembly's stated reason. It is a moral and political preamble, not a finding of fact inside a criminal judgment. The Nuremberg principles, on their own cards, are a different instrument: principles of international criminal law drawn from the tribunal, adopted as a text by the International Law Commission in 1950.

**Fact:** the date, the resolution identifier, the status the UN page gives the declaration, and the two articles quoted.

**Not settled by the proclamation:** that every state observes the articles. The page describes a standard and a later treaty practice. Observance is an empirical question this card does not measure.
